claim: Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) is targeted in the treatment of B-cell disorders including leukemias and lymphomas.
source: Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) is targeted in the treatment of B-cell disorders including leukemias and lymphomas.
evidence: This is a statement of established medical practice supported by the broader scientific literature.

claim: Currently approved BTK inhibitors, including Ibrutinib, bind directly to the kinase active site.
source: Currently approved BTK inhibitors, including Ibrutinib, a first-in-class covalent inhibitor of BTK, bind directly to the kinase active site.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge of BTK inhibitor mechanisms and crystallographic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A remote Ibrutinib resistance mutation, T316A in the BTK SH2 domain, drives spurious BTK activity by destabilizing the compact autoinhibitory conformation of full-length BTK.
source: Additionally, we find that a remote Ibrutinib resistance mutation, T316A in the BTK SH2 domain, drives spurious BTK activity by destabilizing the compact autoinhibitory conformation of full-length BTK, shifting the conformational ensemble away from the autoinhibited form.
evidence: This claim is supported by HDX-MS and NMR data presented in the manuscript showing conformational changes and increased activity for the T316A mutant.

claim: BTK is a non-receptor tyrosine kinase belonging to the TEC family.
source: Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) is a non-receptor tyrosine kinase belonging to the TEC family (Rawlings and Witte, 1995; Berg et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: BTK is expressed primarily in B cells and myeloid cells.
source: BTK is expressed primarily in B cells and myeloid cells, where it functions downstream of receptors including the B-cell receptor, Fc receptors, and toll-like receptors (Kurosaki, 2011; López-Herrera et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2012; Hartkamp et al., 2015; Ellmeier et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: B-cell receptor engagement leads to BTK activation via phosphorylation on Y551 in the activation loop.
source: B-cell receptor engagement leads to BTK activation (via phosphorylation on Y551 in the activation loop), which results in the direct phosphorylation and activation of phospholipase C gamma 2 (PLCγ2) triggering calcium flux and subsequent regulation of gene transcription (Kurosaki, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The regulatory SH3 and SH2 domains of BTK assemble into a compact autoinhibitory conformation on the 'distal' surface of the kinase domain, similar to the autoinhibited SRC kinases.
source: Previous work has established that the regulatory SH3 and SH2 domains of BTK assemble into a compact autoinhibitory conformation on the 'distal' surface of the kinase domain, similar to the autoinhibited SRC kinases (Figure 1b; Joseph et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and reference to Figure 1b.

claim: Solution data support an additional autoinhibitory interface on the activation loop face of the kinase domain occupied by the PHTH domain.
source: Solution data support an additional autoinhibitory interface on the activation loop face of the kinase domain occupied by the PHTH domain (Figure 1b; Amatya et al., 2019; Devkota et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and reference to Figure 1b.

claim: Ibrutinib is an irreversible ATP-competitive inhibitor that binds covalently to BTK C481 within the kinase active site.
source: Ibrutinib is an irreversible ATP-competitive inhibitor that binds covalently to BTK C481 within the kinase active site (Figure 1c,d).
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and reference to Figure 1c,d showing the covalent bond.

claim: Crystallographic analysis reveals that Ibrutinib-bound BTK kinase domain adopts an inactive conformation.
source: Crystallographic analysis reveals that Ibrutinib-bound BTK kinase domain adopts an inactive conformation (Bender et al., 2017); the activation loop is collapsed into the active site, the αC-helix is out, the regulatory spine is not assembled, and the conserved Lys/Glu salt bridge is broken (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior crystallographic work and reference to Figure 1d.

claim: Ibrutinib is currently approved for the treatment of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), Mantle cell lymphoma (MCL), Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia, Marginal zone lymphoma (MZL), and chronic graft versus host disease.
source: Ibrutinib is currently approved for the treatment of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), Mantle cell lymphoma (MCL), Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia, Marginal zone lymphoma (MZL) ,and chronic graft versus host disease and is in various stages of clinical trials for the treatment of other B-cell disorders (Bond et al., 2019; Zi et al., 2019; Davids and Brown, 2014; Molica et al., 2020; Treon et al., 2015; Aw and Brown, 2017; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Second-generation BTK inhibitors, acalabrutinib and zanubrutinib, have received FDA approval.
source: More selective, second-generation BTK inhibitors, acalabrutinib and zanubrutinib (Barf et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2016), have since received FDA approval bringing the total number of approved therapies that target BTK to three.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Recent findings demonstrate a possible role for the BTK inhibitor acalabrutinib in treating excessive inflammation in the context of severe COVID-19.
source: Recent findings demonstrate a possible role for the BTK inhibitor acalabrutinib in treating excessive inflammation in the context of severe COVID-19 (Roschewski et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Off-label use of acalabrutinib for hospitalized COVID-19 patients showed normalization of inflammatory markers and decreased oxygen requirements.
source: Off-label use of acalabrutinib for hospitalized COVID-19 patients showed normalization of inflammatory markers and decreased oxygen requirements (Roschewski et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: All BTK inhibitors currently being used or in clinical trials are active site inhibitors.
source: To date, all BTK inhibitors currently being used or in clinal trials are active site inhibitors.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of BTK inhibitor development.

claim: Of the Ibrutinib resistance mutations that have been identified in BTK, all except one (T316A) cluster to the BTK active site.
source: Of the Ibrutinib resistance mutations that have been identified in BTK, all except one (T316A) cluster to the BTK active site (Puła et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The most prevalent Ibrutinib resistance mutation occurs at BTK C481, the residue in the kinase active site that covalently binds to Ibrutinib.
source: The most prevalent mutation occurs at BTK C481, the residue in the kinase active site that covalently binds to Ibrutinib (Figure 1d; Lampson and Brown, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature and reference to Figure 1d.

claim: The BTK C481S mutation and other kinase active site Ibrutinib resistance mutations are thought to interfere with stable Ibrutinib binding.
source: The BTK C481S mutation and other kinase active site Ibrutinib resistance mutations are thought to interfere with stable Ibrutinib binding (Furman et al., 2014; Woyach et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The BTK T316A mutation occurs in the BTK SH2 domain and is the only Ibrutinib resistance mutation that has been identified to date outside of the BTK kinase domain.
source: In contrast, the BTK T316A mutation occurs in the BTK SH2 domain (Figure 1b) and is the only Ibrutinib resistance mutation that has been identified to date outside of the BTK kinase domain (Sharma et al., 2016; Kadri et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and reference to Figure 1b.

claim: The mechanism by which the remote T316A mutation confers Ibrutinib resistance is currently unknown.
source: The mechanism by which the remote T316A mutation confers Ibrutinib resistance is currently unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the manuscript addresses.

claim: Work from other kinase systems have shown that drug binding to the kinase active site can block catalytic activity as expected but can also have unanticipated and important long-range allosteric effects that impact protein/ligand interactions.
source: Importantly, work from other kinase systems have shown that drug binding to the kinase active site can block catalytic activity as expected but can also have unanticipated and important long-range allosteric effects that impact protein/ligand interactions (Sonti et al., 2018; Leonard et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A panel of five BTK inhibitors was assembled based on availability of crystallographic data and commercial availability of each drug.
source: A panel of five BTK inhibitors, Ibrutinib, GDC-0853 (Fenebrutinib), CGI1746, CC-292 (Spebrutinib, AVL-292), and Dasatinib, was assembled based on availability of crystallographic data and commercial availability of each drug.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and selection criteria for the inhibitors studied.

claim: All inhibitors in this study, except Dasatinib, have been developed as BTK-specific inhibitors.
source: All inhibitors in this study, except Dasatinib, have been developed as BTK-specific inhibitors.
evidence: This is a statement about the specificity of the inhibitors used in the study.

claim: Ibrutinib and Dasatinib have profound effects on the entire BTK protein that extend beyond the active site.
source: We find that Ibrutinib and Dasatinib have profound effects on the entire BTK protein that extend beyond the active site.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript supported by NMR and HDX-MS data.

claim: GDC-0853, CGI1746, and CC-292 do not alter the conformational state of the regulatory domains.
source: In contrast, GDC-0853, CGI1746, and CC-292 do not alter the conformational state of the regulatory domains.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript supported by NMR and HDX-MS data.

claim: The T316A resistance mutation destabilizes the autoinhibited conformation of full-length BTK.
source: Additionally, we explore the mechanism of action of the T316A resistance mutation. This single remote amino acid mutation destabilizes the autoinhibited conformation of full-length BTK.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript supported by HDX-MS and NMR data.

claim: An increase in the population of active enzyme contributes to the decreased Ibrutinib sensitivity observed in vivo for the T316A mutation.
source: We propose that an increase in the population of active enzyme contributes to the decreased Ibrutinib sensitivity observed in vivo.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A conserved structural switch in the αC-helix of protein kinases plays a crucial role in controlling catalytic activity.
source: A conserved structural switch in the αC-helix of protein kinases plays a crucial role in controlling catalytic activity (Taylor et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The conformational equilibrium between an inactive and active kinase domain involves a switch in the αC-helix between an 'αC-out' and 'αC-in' conformation, respectively, which in turn either breaks or creates a salt bridge between a conserved Lys/Glu pair.
source: The conformational equilibrium between an inactive and active kinase domain involves a switch in the αC-helix between an 'αC-out' and 'αC-in' conformation, respectively, which in turn either breaks or creates a salt bridge between a conserved Lys/Glu pair (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and reference to Figure 2a.

claim: The conformational shift in αC is accompanied by a change in the rotamer conformation of the BTK W395 sidechain.
source: Crystal structures of active and inactive BTK kinase domain show that the conformational shift in αC is accompanied by a change in the rotamer conformation of the BTK W395 sidechain (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data and reference to Figure 2a.

claim: The BTK W395 side chain indole NH resonance can be used to monitor the conformational preference of the BTK kinase domain by solution NMR methods.
source: We have established use of the BTK W395 side chain indole NH resonance to monitor the conformational preference of the BTK kinase domain by solution NMR methods (Joseph et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The upfield W395 resonance was previously assigned to the inactive, αC-out conformation.
source: The upfield W395 resonance was previously assigned (Joseph et al., 2017) to the inactive, αC-out conformation and in the full-length apo BTK protein this resonance is in slow exchange with the downfield resonance corresponding to the active, αC-in kinase domain conformation (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work and reference to Figure 2a.

claim: Ibrutinib binding to the BTK kinase domain in solution stabilizes the αC-out conformation observed in the co-crystal structure.
source: To test whether Ibrutinib binding to the BTK kinase domain in solution stabilizes the αC-out conformation observed in the co-crystal structure (Bender et al., 2017), we monitored Ibrutinib binding to the linker-kinase domain fragment of BTK (Figure 1a, LKD, residues 381–659) focusing on the tryptophan indole region of 1H-15N TROSY HSQC spectra (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested by the NMR experiments described and shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The W395 indole NH resonance in the apo BTK LKD is in the downfield position showing that the LKD fragment, in the absence of Ibrutinib, adopts the active or αC-in conformation in solution.
source: The W395 indole NH resonance in the apo BTK LKD is in the downfield position (Figure 2b, top spectrum) showing that the LKD fragment, in the absence of Ibrutinib, adopts the active or αC-in conformation in solution consistent with activity assay results reported previously (Joseph et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2b and a citation to prior activity assay results.

claim: Titration of Ibrutinib into BTK LKD shows an increase in the intensity of the W395 peak in the upfield position, and a corresponding decrease in the intensity of the W395 peak in the downfield position.
source: Titration of Ibrutinib into BTK LKD shows an increase in the intensity of the W395 peak in the upfield position, and a corresponding decrease in the intensity of the W395 peak in the downfield position (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: At a 1:1 molar ratio of protein to drug, the BTK LKD almost exclusively populates the inactive conformation consistent with a single binding site for Ibrutinib.
source: In fact, at a 1:1 molar ratio of protein to drug, the BTK LKD almost exclusively populates the inactive conformation consistent with a single binding site for Ibrutinib (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The intact mass analysis of the full-length BTK:Ibrutinib sample supports the single drug binding site.
source: The intact mass analysis of the full-length BTK:Ibrutinib sample also supports the single drug binding site (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Full-length apo BTK gives rise to more than one W395 resonance indicating exchange between αC-in and αC-out kinase domain conformations likely reflecting the increased conformational heterogeneity in the full-length protein due to the presence of the regulatory domains.
source: As previously reported (Joseph et al., 2017), full-length apo BTK (as compared to the BTK LKD) gives rise to more than one W395 resonance indicating exchange between αC-in and αC-out kinase domain conformations likely reflecting the increased conformational heterogeneity in the full-length protein due to the presence of the regulatory domains (Figure 2d,iii).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2d and a citation to prior work.

claim: Ibrutinib binding to full-length BTK shifts the conformational equilibrium to the αC-out conformation as observed for Ibrutinib-bound LKD.
source: Ibrutinib binding to full-length BTK shifts the conformational equilibrium to the αC-out conformation as observed for Ibrutinib-bound LKD (Figure 2d, iv).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Ibrutinib binding to full-length BTK results in appearance of a new peak corresponding to the indole NH resonance of W251 in the SH3 domain.
source: Ibrutinib binding to full-length BTK also results in appearance of a new peak corresponding to the indole NH resonance of a different tryptophan, W251 in the SH3 domain (Figure 2d, iv, peak denoted with asterisk).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The appearance of the W251 resonance upon addition of Ibrutinib suggests that dynamics in the SH3 domain region have been altered.
source: This resonance is broadened beyond detection in the apo full-length BTK spectrum due to intermediate exchange and so its appearance upon addition of Ibrutinib suggests that dynamics in the SH3 domain region have been altered.
evidence: This is an inference based on the NMR data showing the appearance of the W251 resonance.

claim: The appearance of the W251 resonance in the spectrum of Ibrutinib-bound full-length BTK suggests that drug binding to the kinase active site shifts the conformational preference of the regulatory SH3 domain away from its autoinhibitory contacts on the distal side of the kinase domain.
source: Thus, the appearance of the W251 resonance in the spectrum of Ibrutinib-bound full-length BTK (Figure 2d, iv) suggests that drug binding to the kinase active site shifts the conformational preference of the regulatory SH3 domain away from its autoinhibitory contacts on the distal side of the kinase domain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the NMR data and comparison to the BTK Y223A mutant.

claim: The majority of inhibitors (e.g. Ibrutinib, GDC-0853, CGI1746, and CC-292) stabilize the inactive or αC-out conformation.
source: A comparison of the available structures shows that the majority of inhibitors (e.g. Ibrutinib [irreversible, covalent], GDC-0853 [reversible], CGI1746 [reversible], and CC-292 [irreversible, covalent]) stabilize the inactive or αC-out conformation (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: A key structural feature of the inactive kinase domain includes the activation loop collapsed toward the active site burying the Y551 phosphorylation site.
source: In addition to the αC-out conformation, a key structural feature of the inactive kinase domain includes the activation loop collapsed toward the active site burying the Y551 phosphorylation site.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge of kinase structure.

claim: Electron density is missing for part of the activation loop in the CC-292-BTK structure.
source: In most of the BTK:drug complex structures, the activation loop is resolved but electron density is missing for part of the activation loop in the CC-292-BTK structure (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Superposition of the BTK:Ibrutinib, GDC-0853, CGI1746, and CC-292 complexes shows that the overall conformation of the kinase domain is similar regardless of bound inhibitor.
source: Superposition of these four complexes shows that the overall conformation of the kinase domain is similar regardless of bound inhibitor (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The kinase domain in the Dasatinib-bound complex adopts the active conformation with the αC-helix moved in toward the active site (αC-in) and the activation loop is not visible in the electron density.
source: The Dasatinib-bound structure is different; the kinase domain in this complex adopts the active conformation with the αC-helix moved in toward the active site (αC-in) and the activation loop is not visible in the electron density (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Binding of GDC-0853 and CGI1746 shifts the conformational equilibrium to the inactive (αC-out) conformation in a manner similar to Ibrutinib.
source: We next compared the tryptophan indole region of the 1H-15N TROSY HSQC spectra of apo BTK LKD to BTK LKD bound to the five different active site inhibitors (Figure 4a) and find that binding of GDC-0853 and CGI1746 shifts the conformational equilibrium to the inactive (αC-out) conformation in a manner similar to Ibrutinib (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: In the GDC-0853-bound BTK LKD spectrum, there is a weak W395 peak adjacent to the major W395 peak, indicating that the BTK LKD additionally adopts a minor drug-bound conformation.
source: Interestingly, in the GDC-0853-bound BTK LKD spectrum, there is a weak W395 peak adjacent to the major W395 peak (Figure 4a), indicating that the BTK LKD additionally adopts a minor drug-bound conformation.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Binding of CC-292 to the active site does not shift the conformational preference of the kinase domain in solution toward the αC-out state.
source: Comparison of the tryptophan resonances for apo BTK LKD to BTK LKD bound to CC-292 shows the W395 indole NH resonance remains in the downfield position indicating that binding of CC-292 to the active site does not shift the conformational preference of the kinase domain in solution toward the αC-out state (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The features of the kinase domain that are trapped by crystallography do not accurately represent the conformational ensemble of the CC-292-bound kinase domain in solution.
source: Our results suggest that the features of the kinase domain that are trapped by crystallography (Figure 3a) do not accurately represent the conformational ensemble of the CC-292-bound kinase domain in solution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discrepancy between NMR and crystallographic data.

claim: Crystallography and NMR both indicate Dasatinib-bound BTK adopts the active (αC-in) conformation.
source: Finally, the crystal structure of Dasatinib-bound BTK (Marcotte et al., 2010) is distinct from the other inhibitor-bound structures (Figure 3b–d) and the behavior of the W395 resonance is consistent with the crystal structure. Crystallography and NMR both indicate Dasatinib-bound BTK adopts the active (αC-in) conformation (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by both crystallographic and NMR data.

claim: Dasatinib binding causes a further downfield shift in the 1H resonance frequency of W395 suggesting that either binding of this drug increases the population of the αC-in conformation compared to apo BTK LKD or may be reflective of local chemical shift changes due to drug binding to the active site.
source: Dasatinib binding causes a further downfield shift in the 1H resonance frequency of W395 suggesting that either binding of this drug increases the population of the αC-in conformation compared to apo BTK LKD or may be reflective of local chemical shift changes due to drug binding to the active site.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the NMR data with two possible explanations.

claim: Binding of Ibrutinib, GDC-0853, and CGI1746 all shift the conformational equilibrium of the kinase domain in the full-length protein to the αC-out conformation in a manner that is nearly identical to drug binding to the shorter LKD fragment.
source: Binding of Ibrutinib, GDC-0853, and CGI1746 all shift the conformational equilibrium of the kinase domain in the full-length protein to the αC-out conformation in a manner that is nearly identical to drug binding to the shorter LKD fragment (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The inhibitor-bound W395 indole NH resonances in full-length BTK complexes are more complex with multiple overlapping peaks likely reflecting conformational heterogeneity around the αC-out state of the multi-domain, full-length protein.
source: Although the magnitude and direction of the chemical shift changes are the same for the fragment and full-length BTK, the inhibitor-bound W395 indole NH resonances in these full-length BTK complexes are more complex with multiple overlapping peaks likely reflecting conformational heterogeneity around the αC-out state of the multi-domain, full-length protein (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the NMR data comparing fragment and full-length BTK.

claim: The 1H-15N TROSY HSQC spectrum of full-length BTK bound to CC-292 gives rise to a range of W395 indole NH resonances corresponding to both the αC-in and αC-out states.
source: The 1H-15N TROSY HSQC spectrum of full-length BTK bound to CC-292 gives rise to a range of W395 indole NH resonances corresponding to both the αC-in and αC-out states (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The crystal structure of BTK LKD bound to CC-292 captured the lowest energy, inactive conformation, whereas solution NMR methods reveal the extent of conformational sampling of the CC-292/BTK complex.
source: It is likely that the crystal structure of BTK LKD bound to CC-292 captured the lowest energy, inactive conformation, whereas solution NMR methods reveal the extent of conformational sampling of the CC-292/BTK complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of crystallographic and NMR data.

claim: Dasatinib binding to full-length BTK leads to extensive line-broadening throughout the spectrum.
source: And last, Dasatinib binding to full-length BTK leads to extensive line-broadening throughout the spectrum. The W395 resonance is no longer detected but other resonances remain visible (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The observed line-broadening likely reflects increased dynamics of the conformational ensemble upon Dasatinib binding to the active site.
source: The observed line-broadening likely reflects increased dynamics of the conformational ensemble upon Dasatinib binding to the active site.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the NMR line-broadening data.

claim: The BTK:Dasatinib and BTK:CC-292 complexes both exhibit increased dynamic motions in the kinase domain compared to BTK bound to Ibrutinib, GDC-0853, or CGI1746.
source: While distinctly different from one another, the BTK:Dasatinib and BTK:CC-292 complexes both exhibit increased dynamic motions in the kinase domain compared to BTK bound to Ibrutinib, GDC-0853, or CGI1746.
evidence: This is an inference based on the NMR data for the different complexes.

claim: Ibrutinib labeling of C481 of BTK FL alters deuterium exchange in several different regions of the protein.
source: Comparison of deuterium uptake for Ibrutinib conjugated to full-length BTK with that of apo BTK (Figures 5a and 6) shows that Ibrutinib labeling of C481 of BTK FL alters deuterium exchange in several different regions of the protein.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figures 5a and 6.

claim: The β2 and β3 strands in the kinase N-lobe as well as the β7, β8 strands and the N-terminus of the kinase activation segment (DFG motif) show reduced deuterium incorporation that is consistent with the location of Ibrutinib binding in the kinase active site.
source: As expected, the β2 and β3 strands in the kinase N-lobe as well as the β7, β8 strands and the N-terminus of the kinase activation segment (DFG motif) show reduced deuterium incorporation that is consistent with the location of Ibrutinib binding in the kinase active site (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Despite Ibrutinib stabilizing an inactive (αC-out) conformation in the kinase domain, increases in deuterium exchange are observed in both SH3 and SH2 domains as well as in the SH2-kinase linker, consistent with destabilization of the autoinhibitory interface.
source: Importantly, despite Ibrutinib stabilizing an inactive (αC-out) conformation in the kinase domain, increases in deuterium exchange are observed in both SH3 and SH2 domains as well as in the SH2-kinase linker, consistent with destabilization of the autoinhibitory interface (Figures 5a and 6).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figures 5a and 6.

claim: Ibrutinib binding to the active site favors a 'hybrid' conformational state of full-length BTK: an inactive (αC-out) conformation is stabilized in the kinase domain, while the regulatory domains are at least partially released from the distal surface of the kinase domain to populate an open 'active' conformation.
source: Together, the NMR and HDX-MS data indicate that Ibrutinib binding to the active site favors a 'hybrid' conformational state of full-length BTK: an inactive (αC-out) conformation is stabilized in the kinase domain, while the regulatory domains are at least partially released from the distal surface of the kinase domain to populate an open 'active' conformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined NMR and HDX-MS data.

claim: GDC-0853 and CGI1746 lead to pronounced protection from exchange in the kinase domain but they do not affect the regulatory domains.
source: Despite the strong similarities between the W395 resonance frequencies (Figure 4) and the crystal structures of Ibrutinib, GDC-0853, and CGI1746 bound to the BTK kinase domain (Figure 3a,b), the HDX-MS data show that GDC-0853 and CGI1746 lead to pronounced protection from exchange in the kinase domain but they do not affect the regulatory domains (Figures 5b,c and 6).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figures 5b,c and 6.

claim: Upon binding of GDC-0853 and CGI1746 the activation loop is more strongly protected than when bound to Ibrutinib.
source: Specifically, upon binding of GDC-0853 and CGI1746 the activation loop (e.g. Figure 5b,c, peptide iv) is more strongly protected than when bound to Ibrutinib while parts of the αF and αG helices are strongly protected with GDC-0853 and CGI1746 but not protected at all by Ibrutinib (Figures 5a,b,c and 6).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Peptides that cover β1–3 in the N-lobe of the kinase domain are both sensitive to the presence of the inhibitor and see an attenuation in the degree of that protection as the regulatory domains are released from the autoinhibited conformation.
source: It is also important to note that peptides that cover β1–3 in the N-lobe of the kinase domain (e.g. Figure 5, peptide iii) are both sensitive to the presence of the inhibitor (protection from exchange in the inhibitor-bound forms compared to the apo-form) and see an attenuation in the degree of that protection (difference between BTK:Ibrutinib and BTK:GDC-0853/CGI1746) as the regulatory domains are released from the autoinhibited conformation.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 5.

claim: There are clear conformational differences in the BTK regulatory domains between the drug-bound forms in solution.
source: While the HDX-MS changes within the kinase domain are consistent with the binding mode and contacts being made by the drug within the BTK active site in the BTK:drug co-crystals (Figure 3b), HDX-MS of full-length BTK reveals that there are clear conformational differences in the BTK regulatory domains between the drug-bound forms in solution.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the HDX-MS data.

claim: HDX-MS reveals only limited protection upon CC-292 binding localized primarily to the N-lobe surrounding the active site.
source: While CC-292 is covalently attached to BTK C481 and contacts the hinge region of the kinase, it does not extend further into the kinase active site setting it apart from the other BTK inhibitors (Figure 3). Consistent with this, HDX-MS reveals only limited protection upon CC-292 binding localized primarily to the N-lobe surrounding the active site (Figure 5d, peptide iii, 6).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figures 5d and 6.

claim: The lack of protection from deuterium exchange in the activation loop of BTK upon binding to CC-292 is consistent with high flexibility and the absence of electron density for this region in the crystal structure of CC-292 bound to BTK LKD.
source: The lack of protection from deuterium exchange in the activation loop of BTK upon binding to CC-292 is consistent with high flexibility and the absence of electron density for this region in the crystal structure of CC-292 bound to BTK LKD (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is an inference connecting HDX-MS data to crystallographic observations.

claim: The BTK:CC-292 complex, like the GDC-0853 and CGI1746 complexes, is characterized by a lack of changes in the regulatory domains.
source: Finally, the BTK:CC-292 complex, like the GDC-0853 and CGI1746 complexes, is characterized by a lack of changes in the regulatory domains.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data.

claim: Binding of GDC-0853, CGI1746, and CC-292 do not shift the equilibrium away from the inactive, autoinhibited conformation of full-length BTK.
source: As full-length BTK is predominantly in the autoinhibited conformation in solution (Joseph et al., 2017), this result indicates that binding of GDC-0853, CGI1746, and CC-292 do not shift the equilibrium away from the inactive, autoinhibited conformation of full-length BTK.
evidence: This is an inference based on the HDX-MS data and prior knowledge of BTK conformation.

claim: HDX-MS of the BTK:Dasatinib complex shows that this complex exhibits the largest differences compared to apo full-length BTK.
source: HDX-MS of the BTK:Dasatinib complex shows that this complex exhibits the largest differences compared to apo full-length BTK (Figures 5e and 6).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figures 5e and 6.

claim: Dasatinib binding causes dramatic increased deuterium uptake in a large part of the kinase domain C-lobe and activation loop, suggesting that these regions of the protein become less structured and more solvent exposed upon binding to Dasatinib.
source: In contrast to the other BTK:drug complexes, Dasatinib binding causes dramatic increased deuterium uptake in a large part of the kinase domain C-lobe and activation loop (Figure 5e, peptide iv, 6), a result suggesting that these regions of the protein become less structured and more solvent exposed upon binding to Dasatinib.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figures 5e and 6.

claim: The SH3 and SH2 domains and the SH2-kinase linker region all exhibit increased deuteration upon Dasatinib binding to the BTK active site.
source: In addition, the SH3 and SH2 domains and the SH2-kinase linker region all exhibit increased deuteration upon Dasatinib binding to the BTK active site (Figures 5e and 6) and the extent of deuterium uptake is greater than that observed for Ibrutinib binding suggesting Dasatinib shifts the population away from the autoinhibited form to a greater extent than Ibrutinib (Figure 5a,e, peptide i and 6).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figures 5e and 6.

claim: Dasatinib shifts the population away from the autoinhibited form to a greater extent than Ibrutinib.
source: In addition, the SH3 and SH2 domains and the SH2-kinase linker region all exhibit increased deuteration upon Dasatinib binding to the BTK active site (Figures 5e and 6) and the extent of deuterium uptake is greater than that observed for Ibrutinib binding suggesting Dasatinib shifts the population away from the autoinhibited form to a greater extent than Ibrutinib (Figure 5a,e, peptide i and 6).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of HDX-MS data for Dasatinib and Ibrutinib.

claim: The W395 resonance suggests that the kinase domain in the Dasatinib:BTK complex populates the αC-in conformation rather than the αC-out conformation stabilized by Ibrutinib providing a possible explanation for how Dasatinib induces greater exposure in the regulatory domains.
source: Indeed, the W395 resonance suggests that the kinase domain in the Dasatinib:BTK complex populates the αC-in conformation rather than the αC-out conformation stabilized by Ibrutinib providing a possible explanation for how Dasatinib induces greater exposure in the regulatory domains.
evidence: This is an inference connecting NMR and HDX-MS data.

claim: Ibrutinib and Dasatinib promote changes in the conformational equilibria of full-length BTK, whereas the other inhibitors, GDC-0853, CGI1746, and CC-292, cause significantly more localized conformational adjustments limited to the kinase domain.
source: Taking the results for all the inhibitors together, NMR and HDX-MS data provide unique insights into the extent to which different BTK inhibitors affect the conformational preferences and dynamics of both the kinase domain itself and the regulatory domains within full-length BTK. Ibrutinib and Dasatinib promote changes in the conformational equilibria of full-length BTK, whereas the other inhibitors, GDC-0853, CGI1746, and CC-292, cause significantly more localized conformational adjustments limited to the kinase domain.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the combined NMR and HDX-MS data.

claim: T316 is adjacent to R307, a key residue in the autoinhibitory salt bridge interaction between the SH2 domain and D656 in the C-terminus of the kinase domain.
source: T316 is adjacent to R307, a key residue in the autoinhibitory salt bridge interaction between the SH2 domain and D656 in the C-terminus of the kinase domain (Figure 7a,b; Joseph et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 7a,b and a citation to prior work.

claim: Based on the crystal structure of this region of autoinhibited BTK, T316 is predicted to stabilize the productive autoinhibitory conformation of the R307 sidechain via a network of hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic, and cation-pi contacts involving R288, R307, S309, H333, D656, and E658.
source: Based on the crystal structure of this region of autoinhibited BTK (Wang et al., 2015), T316 is predicted to stabilize the productive autoinhibitory conformation of the R307 sidechain via a network of hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic, and cation-pi contacts involving R288, R307, S309, H333, D656, and E658 (Figure 7a,b).
evidence: This is an inference based on the crystal structure and a citation to prior work.

claim: Loss of even the small threonine side chain could be deleterious to this local structure and lead to a conformational change that is propagated across the autoinhibitory interface involving the entire SH3-SH2-linker region, thereby activating BTK.
source: Loss of even the small threonine side chain could be deleterious to this local structure and lead to a conformational change that is propagated across the autoinhibitory interface involving the entire SH3-SH2-linker region, thereby activating BTK.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the mechanism of the T316A mutation.

claim: Comparing the extent of deuterium uptake for wild-type BTK versus the T316A mutant shows small increases in exchange in the non-catalytic regulatory SH3-SH2 region upon mutation of T316 to alanine.
source: Comparing the extent of deuterium uptake for wild-type BTK versus the T316A mutant shows small increases in exchange in the non-catalytic regulatory SH3-SH2 region upon mutation of T316 to alanine (Figure 7c,d).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 7c,d.

claim: The regions affected by the T316A mutation in the SH2 domain localize to the SH3-SH2 domains and SH2-kinase linker that together create autoinhibitory contacts with the distal side of the kinase domain.
source: Mapping the peptides that show increased deuterium uptake for the BTK T316A mutant onto the autoinhibited structure shows that the regions affected by the mutation in the SH2 domain localize to the SH3-SH2 domains and SH2-kinase linker that together create autoinhibitory contacts with the distal side of the kinase domain (Figure 7e).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 7e.

claim: The changes observed for the T316A mutation are consistent with a more transiently populated 'open' conformation compared to the more drastic changes in deuterium uptake observed upon mutation of D656 in previous work.
source: As well, the changes observed for the T316A mutation are consistent with a more transiently populated 'open' conformation compared to the more drastic changes in deuterium uptake observed upon mutation of D656 in previous work (Joseph et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of HDX-MS data for T316A and D656 mutations.

claim: The BTK C481S active site resistance mutant shows no change in exchange behavior compared to the wild-type protein.
source: In contrast to the changes in deuterium exchange observed for the BTK T316A mutant, the BTK C481S active site resistance mutant shows no change in exchange behavior compared to the wild-type protein (Figure 7d, Source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: The T316A mutation in the BTK SH2 domain shifts the conformational ensemble of BTK toward the active kinase (αC-in) population.
source: NMR analysis confirms that the T316A mutation in the BTK SH2 domain shifts the conformational ensemble of BTK toward the active kinase (αC-in) population.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data.

claim: 72% of full-length wild-type BTK adopts a conformation consistent with inactive kinase (αC-out) and mutation of T316 to alanine results in only 60% of the full-length kinase in an inactive conformation.
source: Comparing the 1H-15N TROSY HSQC spectrum of the full-length BTK T316A to wild-type BTK shows a change in the conformational equilibrium upon mutation (Figure 8a). Peak intensities for the W395 resonance in the upfield and downfield positions indicate that 72% of full-length wild-type BTK adopts a conformation consistent with inactive kinase (αC-out) and mutation of T316 to alanine results in only 60% of the full-length kinase in an inactive conformation.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 8a.

claim: The population of active BTK as measured by W395 peak intensity increases ~1.5-fold, from 28% for wild-type BTK to 40% for the BTK T316A mutant.
source: Accordingly, the population of active BTK as measured by W395 peak intensity increases ~1.5-fold, from 28% for wild-type BTK to 40% for the BTK T316A mutant (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 8a.

claim: Phosphorylation on Y551 in the BTK T316A activation loop is twice that of wild-type BTK consistent with the shift in the conformational ensemble measured by NMR.
source: To directly test kinase activity, we compared autophosphorylation of BTK wild-type and T316A mutant under identical kinase assay conditions. Phosphorylation on Y551 in the BTK T316A activation loop is twice that of wild-type BTK consistent with the shift in the conformational ensemble measured by NMR (Figure 8b,c).
evidence: This is supported by kinase activity assay data shown in Figure 8b,c.

claim: No difference in kinase activity is observed between wild-type BTK and the C481S mutant.
source: BTK C481S mutant is included the kinase assay and, as predicted by the identical deuterium exchange behavior of this mutant compared to wild-type, no difference in kinase activity is observed between wild-type BTK and the C481S mutant (Figure 8b,c).
evidence: This is supported by kinase activity assay data shown in Figure 8b,c.

claim: The remote T316A resistance mutation in the BTK SH2 domain leads to an increase in the population of active enzyme that is reflected by an increase in activity.
source: Thus, the remote T316A resistance mutation in the BTK SH2 domain leads to an increase in the population of active enzyme that is reflected by an increase in activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined NMR and kinase activity data.

claim: W395 reports a shift toward the inactive (αC-out) kinase domain conformation upon Ibrutinib binding to the BTK T316A mutant that mirrors the results of Ibrutinib binding to wild-type BTK.
source: W395 reports a shift toward the inactive (αC-out) kinase domain conformation upon Ibrutinib binding to the BTK T316A mutant that mirrors the results of Ibrutinib binding to wild-type BTK (Figure 8d).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 8d.

claim: Ibrutinib binding to the T316A mutant results in increased deuterium exchange in the region spanning the SH3, SH2 domains and SH2-kinase linker in a manner that is nearly identical to wild-type protein.
source: Ibrutinib binding to the T316A mutant results in increased deuterium exchange in the region spanning the SH3, SH2 domains and SH2-kinase linker in a manner that is nearly identical to wild-type protein (Figure 8e, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 8e.

claim: The Ibrutinib-induced remote conformational changes in the regulatory region of BTK appear to be a general consequence of Ibrutinib binding that occurs regardless of the T316A mutation in the BTK SH2 domain.
source: Thus, the Ibrutinib-induced remote conformational changes in the regulatory region of BTK appear to be a general consequence of Ibrutinib binding that occurs regardless of the T316A mutation in the BTK SH2 domain.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the HDX-MS data comparing wild-type and T316A mutant.

claim: No meaningful differences (>0.5 Da) in deuterium uptake are observed between wild-type BTK and the BTK T316A mutant over a range of Ibrutinib concentrations.
source: To assess whether the T316A mutation in the SH2 domain affects drug binding to the active site, we instead performed an HDX-MS titration series to compare Ibrutinib binding to wild-type and T316A BTK. No meaningful differences (>0.5 Da) in deuterium uptake are observed between wild-type BTK and the BTK T316A mutant over a range of Ibrutinib concentrations (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS titration data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: The BTK T316A mutation likely causes resistance to Ibrutinib by shifting the conformational ensemble of full-length BTK to favor the active state.
source: Thus, our results indicate that the BTK T316A mutation likely causes resistance to Ibrutinib (Sharma et al., 2016) by shifting the conformational ensemble of full-length BTK to favor the active state.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined data and a citation to prior work showing resistance.

claim: At concentrations of Ibrutinib that exceed the IC50, there is no evidence that the T316A mutation in the SH2 domain limits binding of drug to the BTK active site.
source: At concentrations of Ibrutinib that exceed the IC50, there is no evidence that the T316A mutation in the SH2 domain limits binding of drug to the BTK active site.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the HDX-MS titration data.

claim: The occupancy of the kinase active site by different inhibitors can have profoundly distinct effects on the distant BTK regulatory domains, effects that are missed in crystal structures of drug-bound kinase domain alone.
source: The essential role that kinases play in cell signaling make them attractive pharmacological targets (Zhao and Bourne, 2018; Müller et al., 2015). The vast majority of available kinase inhibitors target the kinase active site and our work shows that the occupancy of the kinase active site by different inhibitors can have profoundly distinct effects on the distant BTK regulatory domains, effects that are missed in crystal structures of drug-bound kinase domain alone.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the manuscript.

claim: Approval of an increasing number of covalent inhibitors demonstrate the effectiveness of irreversible drugs compared to reversible inhibitors in the targeted therapies of kinases.
source: Approval of an increasing number of covalent inhibitors demonstrate the effectiveness of irreversible drugs compared to reversible inhibitors in the targeted therapies of kinases (Zhao and Bourne, 2018; Bauer, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A major advantage of irreversible inhibitors is that once covalently bound to the kinase, they permanently trap the protein, thereby sequestering its catalytic function until fresh protein is produced by translation.
source: A major advantage of irreversible inhibitors is that once covalently bound to the kinase, they permanently trap the protein, thereby sequestering its catalytic function until fresh protein is produced by translation (Barf and Kaptein, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Covalent inhibitors are selected for rapid clearance from the serum to prevent toxicity effects arising from off-target modification.
source: Additionally, covalent inhibitors are selected for rapid clearance from the serum to prevent toxicity effects arising from off-target modification (Barf and Kaptein, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Ibrutinib levels in the serum peak 1–2 hr post-ingestion and return to basal levels after 3–4 hr.
source: Ibrutinib levels in the serum peak 1–2 hr post-ingestion and return to basal levels after 3–4 hr (Advani et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The BTK C481S resistance mutation prevents the covalent attachment of Ibrutinib to the active site during the period when Ibrutinib is available in the serum but Ibrutinib still binds noncovalently.
source: The BTK C481S resistance mutation prevents the covalent attachment of Ibrutinib to the active site during the period when Ibrutinib is available in the serum but Ibrutinib still binds noncovalently (Furman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Once serum Ibrutinib levels diminish, BTK signaling by the BTK C481S mutant occurs resulting in drug resistance.
source: This reversible drug binding coupled with rapid serum clearance implies that the BTK C481S mutant is not 'trapped' by Ibrutinib. Once serum Ibrutinib levels diminish, BTK signaling by the BTK C481S mutant occurs resulting in drug resistance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the C481S mutation and Ibrutinib pharmacokinetics.

claim: When the BTK T316A mutant encounters Ibrutinib it is likely 'trapped' by the covalent drug in a manner similar to wild-type BTK.
source: The BTK T316A resistance mutant retains the ability to be covalently modified by Ibrutinib. Thus, when the BTK T316A mutant encounters Ibrutinib it is likely 'trapped' by the covalent drug in a manner similar to wild-type BTK.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing Ibrutinib binding to T316A.

claim: Newly synthesized BTK T316A could escape the narrow inhibition time window created by rapid Ibrutinib clearance.
source: However, the BTK T316A mutation is itself activating; loss of the T316 sidechain destabilizes a key down-regulatory interaction within BTK and shifts the conformational equilibrium away from the autoinhibited state (Figures 7c and 8a). And so, newly synthesized BTK T316A could escape the narrow inhibition time window created by rapid Ibrutinib clearance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the activating nature of the T316A mutation and Ibrutinib pharmacokinetics.

claim: The unconjugated and active T316A mutant could then promote BTK signaling, unlike properly autoinhibited wild-type BTK.
source: The unconjugated and active T316A mutant could then promote BTK signaling, unlike properly autoinhibited wild-type BTK.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism of resistance.

claim: The idea that resistance mutations can counteract the autoinhibitory state has been elegantly demonstrated in recently published work on the ABL kinase.
source: The idea that resistance mutations can counteract the autoinhibitory state has been elegantly demonstrated in recently published work on the ABL kinase (Xie et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: It is possible that phosphorylated BTK T316A could exhibit diminished affinity for Ibrutinib thereby also contributing to the observed resistance.
source: It should be noted that we have not characterized binding of Ibrutinib to the phosphorylated form of BTK and so it is possible that phosphorylated BTK T316A could exhibit diminished affinity for Ibrutinib thereby also contributing to the observed resistance.
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative mechanism that was not tested.

claim: Binding of either Ibrutinib or Dasatinib triggers a shift in the conformational equilibrium of the regulatory domains away from the autoinhibited conformation creating the opportunity for BTK regulatory domain interactions with exogenous ligands despite the inhibited kinase domain.
source: Our findings now show that mutation is not the only mechanism by which the BTK conformational ensemble shifts away from the 'closed' autoinhibited state. Binding of either Ibrutinib or Dasatinib triggers the same shift in the conformational equilibrium of the regulatory domains away from the autoinhibited conformation creating the opportunity for BTK regulatory domain interactions with exogenous ligands despite the inhibited kinase domain.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: This conformational shift could promote kinase-independent signaling events and/or create a dominant negative.
source: This conformational shift could promote kinase-independent signaling events (Saito et al., 2003; Middendorp et al., 2003; Middendorp et al., 2005) and/or create a dominant negative.
evidence: This is speculation about potential functional consequences supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Varied effects of inhibitor binding on the non-catalytic functions of kinases have been observed previously and range from alterations in interactions with upstream or downstream regulatory kinases and phosphatases to changes in ligand affinity.
source: Varied effects of inhibitor binding on the non-catalytic functions of kinases have been observed previously and range from alterations in interactions with upstream or downstream regulatory kinases and phosphatases to changes in ligand affinity (Sonti et al., 2018; Leonard et al., 2014; Tong et al., 2017; Skora et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

source: For BTK specifically, recent evidence suggests that non-catalytic functions of Ibrutinib-bound BTK activate CLL-specific PLCγ variants (Wist et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Selection of BTK inhibitor type to treat specific disease states as well as design of the next generation of BTK inhibitors need to carefully consider the impact of the inhibitor on BTK regulatory domain conformation.
source: Thus, selection of BTK inhibitor type to treat specific disease states as well as design of the next generation of BTK inhibitors need to carefully consider the impact of the inhibitor on BTK regulatory domain conformation.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the manuscript.

claim: Of the five active site inhibitors studied here only CGI1746, CC-292, and GDC-0853 inhibit kinase activity without disrupting the autoinhibitory conformation of the full-length kinase.
source: Of the five active site inhibitors studied here only CGI1746, CC-292, and GDC-0853 inhibit kinase activity without disrupting the autoinhibitory conformation of the full-length kinase.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ibrutinib and Dasatinib alter the conformational equilibrium of the multidomain kinase decreasing the population of the autoinhibited kinase even though the drugs block and inactivate the kinase domain.
source: Ibrutinib and Dasatinib alter the conformational equilibrium of the multidomain kinase decreasing the population of the autoinhibited kinase even though the drugs block and inactivate the kinase domain.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The effect of an active site inhibitor on the overall conformational preference of a multidomain kinase must originate in the kinase domain.
source: The effect of an active site inhibitor on the overall conformational preference of a multidomain kinase must originate in the kinase domain.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the mechanism of allosteric effects.

claim: Multiple mobile elements including the αC-helix, DFG motif, and the activation loop switch the kinase domain between its inactive and active conformations.
source: Multiple mobile elements including the αC-helix, DFG motif, and the activation loop switch the kinase domain between its inactive and active conformations (Taylor et al., 2015; Taylor and Kornev, 2011; Fabbro et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: For the SRC family, the αC-in configuration has been correlated with release of the regulatory domains from the autoinhibited state.
source: For the SRC family, the αC-in configuration has been correlated with release of the regulatory domains from the autoinhibited state (Leonard et al., 2014; Tsutsui et al., 2016).

source: Other studies suggest that the αC-helix conformation alone can be used to predict the regulatory domain conformation in the SRC, ABL, and TEC kinases; inhibitors that stabilize the αC-in conformation disrupt the regulatory domains from their autoinhibitory conformation, whereas αC-out stabilizing inhibitors do not (Fang, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: ABL focused studies show that Dasatinib stabilizes αC-in but does not disrupt the regulatory domains from their compact, autoinhibitory state.
source: However, ABL focused studies show that Dasatinib stabilizes αC-in but does not disrupt the regulatory domains from their compact, autoinhibitory state (Sonti et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: For ABL, a strict correlation has been observed between activation loop conformation and regulatory domain assembly.
source: For ABL, a strict correlation has been observed instead between activation loop conformation and regulatory domain assembly (Sonti et al., 2018; Skora et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Inhibitors that stabilize an activation loop 'in' conformation disrupt the ABL SH3 and SH2 domains from their autoinhibited conformation, whereas inhibitors that stabilize the activation loop 'out' conformation do not.
source: Inhibitors that stabilize an activation loop 'in' conformation disrupt the ABL SH3 and SH2 domains from their autoinhibited conformation, whereas inhibitors that stabilize the activation loop 'out' conformation do not.
evidence: This is a statement about findings in ABL kinase studies.

claim: Simple αC-helix or activation loop 'in' versus 'out' metrics are not sufficient to explain BTK inhibitor effects.
source: Our results suggest simple αC-helix or activation loop 'in' versus 'out' metrics are not sufficient to explain BTK inhibitor effects.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both Ibrutinib and CGI1746 favor the activation loop 'in' configuration, but the regulatory domains are displaced upon Ibrutinib binding and remain in the autoinhibited conformation on binding CGI1746.
source: Just one example from the data presented here shows that both Ibrutinib and CGI1746 favor the activation loop 'in' configuration, but the regulatory domains are displaced upon Ibrutinib binding and remain in the autoinhibited conformation on binding CGI1746.
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: There are two distinct drug orientations among the five BTK:drug complexes.
source: To understand why Ibrutinib and Dasatinib disrupt the autoinhibited conformation of full-length BTK while GDC-0853, CGI1746, and CC-292 do not, we turn back to the crystal structures of BTK LKD bound to each inhibitor (Figure 3). Probing for features that are common to the Ibrutinib- and Dasatinib-bound structures but distinct from the other inhibitor-bound structures, we observed two distinct drug orientations among the five BTK:drug complexes (Figure 9a,b).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of crystal structures shown in Figure 9a,b.

claim: The orientations of Ibrutinib and Dasatinib differ significantly from that of GDC-0853, CGI1746, and CC-292.
source: Interestingly, the orientations of Ibrutinib and Dasatinib (the two inhibitors that disrupt the full-length BTK autoinhibitory structure), differ significantly from that of GDC-0853, CGI1746, and CC-292 (Figure 9a,b).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of crystal structures shown in Figure 9a,b.

claim: Ibrutinib and Dasatinib are oriented toward the 'back pocket' of the kinase active site, whereas GDC-0853, CGI1764, and CC-292 bypass the back pocket and extend into the front pocket toward the activation loop.
source: Ibrutinib and Dasatinib are oriented toward the 'back pocket' of the kinase active site (also called the back cleft or hydrophobic pocket II (HPII)) (Roskoski, 2016), whereas GDC-0853, CGI1764, and CC-292 bypass the back pocket and extend into the front pocket toward the activation loop (Figure 9a,b).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of crystal structures shown in Figure 9a,b.

claim: All five compounds maintain contacts with the kinase hinge region.
source: All five compounds maintain contacts with the kinase hinge region (Figure 9a).

claim: In accessing the back pocket of the active site, Ibrutinib and Dasatinib alter the back pocket around the regulatory (R-) spine residue L460.
source: In accessing the back pocket of the active site, Ibrutinib and Dasatinib alter the back pocket around the regulatory (R-) spine (Taylor et al., 2015; Kornev and Taylor, 2010; Kornev et al., 2008) residue L460 (Figure 9c).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of crystal structures shown in Figure 9c.

source: Ibrutinib directly contacts L460, while Dasatinib binding induces the inward movement of the αC-helix bringing M449 in direct contact with L460 (Figure 9c).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of crystal structures shown in Figure 9c.

claim: The compounds that extend into the front pocket, such as GDC-0853, avoid all contact, direct or indirect with L460.
source: In contrast, the compounds that extend into the front pocket, such as GDC-0853 (Figure 9c), avoid all contact, direct or indirect with L460.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of crystal structures shown in Figure 9c.

claim: L460 is adjacent to Y461, a component of the conserved 'hydrophobic stack'.
source: L460 is adjacent to Y461, a component of the conserved 'hydrophobic stack'.
evidence: This is supported by structural knowledge.

claim: The 'hydrophobic stack' consists of two residues on the distal surface of the kinase domain (Y461 and W421 in BTK) and a single hydrophobic residue from the linker spanning the SH2 and kinase domains (L390 in BTK).
source: The 'hydrophobic stack' consists of two residues on the distal surface of the kinase domain (Y461 and W421 in BTK) and a single hydrophobic residue from the linker spanning the SH2 and kinase domains (L390 in BTK) (Figure 9a).
evidence: This is supported by structural knowledge and reference to Figure 9a.

claim: Regulatory domain release from the distal side of the kinase domain leads to disruption of the hydrophobic stack and is accompanied by exchange of ADP for ATP in the active site, thus linking the conformational preference of the regulatory domains and the occupancy of the active site.
source: Regulatory domain release from the distal side of the kinase domain leads to disruption of the hydrophobic stack and is accompanied by exchange of ADP for ATP in the active site, thus linking the conformational preference of the regulatory domains and the occupancy of the active site (von Raußendorf et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Small molecules that fill (directly or indirectly) the back pocket of the active site, may allosterically trigger conformational adjustments in the hydrophobic stack region that result in displacement of the regulatory domains from their autoinhibited pose.
source: Given the impact of Ibrutinib and Dasatinib on the R-spine residue L460 and the fact that the hydrophobic stack residue Y461 is adjacent to L460, we can speculate that small molecules that fill (directly or indirectly) the back pocket of the active site, may allosterically trigger conformational adjustments in the hydrophobic stack region that result in displacement of the regulatory domains from their autoinhibited pose.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural observations.

claim: This is a new metric for predicting global conformational effects of specific BTK inhibitors that does not depend on strict conformational requirements being met in the αC helix and/or activation loop.
source: This is a new metric for predicting global conformational effects of specific BTK inhibitors that does not depend on strict conformational requirements being met in the αC helix and/or activation loop.
evidence: This is a proposed new framework based on the findings of the manuscript.

source: Structural studies that combine data from X-ray crystallography, solution NMR and HDX-MS provide a detailed and more complete picture to identify key regulatory interactions at work in protein kinases.

claim: Use of the full-length kinase reveals unexpected differences between BTK inhibitors that are missed in crystallographic analyses of fragments.

source: For BTK, this work has demonstrated that the clinically important inhibitor Ibrutinib imposes conformational adjustments on the distant non-catalytic domains of BTK, which may be functionally relevant in vivo.

claim: BTK inhibitors that do not induce a conformational shift toward the 'open' form of BTK may improve the efficacy of disease treatment where the kinase-independent functions of BTK play an important role.
